Title: Generally Available: Cost management and tagging for Claude models in Microsoft Foundry

Body.Content:
Microsoft Foundry now brings Claude models into Azure Cost Management alongside the rest of your Foundry spend, generally available. Until now, Claude charges appeared under SaaS rather than under the Foundry resource used to deploy them, and Claude deployments lacked the tags enterprises rely on for showback and chargeback, leaving finance and platform teams to reconcile costs by hand. With this release, Claude costs appear under the associated Foundry resource; Claude deployments and Foundry resources support tags that follow your organization's existing conventions; and Claude cost records carry model and usage_type tags, so you can filter and group spending by Claude model and separate input-token from output-token costs. Customers get one consistent, resource-level view of Claude spending and can allocate usage to the responsible teams and workloads without a separate reconciliation process. To get started, open Cost analysis in Azure Cost Management and group by resource or tag. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Azure Front Door profile and route level WAF policies

Body.Content:
Announcing the general availability of profile and route level policies for Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) on Azure Front Door Premium. WAF policies are no longer limited to individual domains: you can now apply broad baseline protection across an entire Azure Front Door profile and use targeted policies for the routes that need different controls.   

You can associate a WAF policy at the profile, domain, or route scope. For example, use a profile level policy for common protections across every domain in a profile, then apply a route level policy to sensitive paths such as sign-in, checkout, or API routes. This reduces policy duplication for teams that run many applications behind a single Azure Front Door profile, while keeping granular controls where they're needed.   

When more than one scope applies to a request, Azure Front Door uses the most specific policy: a route level policy takes precedence over a domain level policy, and a domain level policy takes precedence over a profile level policy. Existing domain level associations continue to work without any changes.   

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Network Watcher VNet flow logs filtering

Body.Content:
Azure Network Watcher VNet flow logs filtering is now generally available, enabling you to control which network traffic flows are logged based on specific criteria such as IP addresses, ports, protocols, encryption state, flow state, and traffic direction. 

With this capability, you can focus logging on the traffic that matters most for monitoring, troubleshooting, security, compliance, and network optimization. Filtering helps reduce log volume by capturing only relevant flows, which can lower storage costs and make analysis easier by reducing noise. 

This feature is now accessible through the Azure portal, in addition to PowerShell, making it easier to configure and manage filtering for VNet flow logs directly from the portal. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Item Level Recovery for Azure VMs with Premium SSDv2 and Ultra Disks in Azure Backup

Body.Content:
Azure Backup now supports Item-Level Recovery (ILR) for Azure virtual machines using Premium SSD v2 and Ultra disks with both 512 byte and 4KB logical sector sizes. You can now recover individual files and folders from your Azure VMs with Premium SSDv2 and Ultra disks. 

You can generate a file-recovery executable or script through the Azure portal, CLI, or PowerShell, then run it on a compatible machine to access the recovery point, selectively browse, and copy individual files or folders without performing a full disk or virtual machine restore, in parity with the existing ILR behavior. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: ABFS Vectored Read for Azure Data Lake Storage

Body.Content:
ABFS Vectored Read helps compatible analytics engines reduce request overhead for selective reads in Azure Data Lake Storage. By combining nearby file ranges into fewer storage requests and executing reads asynchronously, it can reduce network round trips for workloads such as selective Parquet queries.

Compatible Spark workloads can enable the capability through configuration, without rewriting queries or migrating data.

Learn more.

Title: Announcing: Choose Your Own Telephony (CYOT) for Microsoft Entra

Body.Content:
What and why

Starting October 30, 2026, Microsoft Entra ID will make the Choose Your Own Telephony Provider experience available. This feature enables organizations to use a supported third-party telecommunications provider for SMS and voice authentication. Organizations select a supported provider through Microsoft Security Store and manage their commercial relationship directly with the provider.

Microsoft recommends phishing-resistant authentication methods, such as passkeys, instead of SMS or voice authentication. Organizations should use a telephony provider for user populations that have a business, regulatory, or technical requirement for telephony-based authentication.

Starting October 30, 2026, organizations can choose to enable CYOT. Organizations planning to adopt CYOT should begin preparing before October 30. Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication are scheduled to begin retiring on February 1, 2027.

What you need to do to prepare

If your organization plans to adopt CYOT, we recommend preparing the following ahead of its targeted GA date of October 30, 2026:

  1. Identify the users who require SMS or voice authentication. Determine which user populations have a documented business, regulatory, or technical requirement for telephony-based authentication.

  2. Evaluate phishing-resistant alternatives. Confirm that a phishing-resistant authentication method does not meet the requirements for these users.

  3. Review supported telephony providers. Compare providers based on geographic coverage, supported delivery channels, pricing, support, security, and compliance capabilities.

  4. Review organizational requirements. Work with the appropriate teams in your organization to review procurement, privacy, and regulatory requirements before selecting a provider.

  5. Plan your transition. Review the guidance for the retirement of Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication and plan your deployment accordingly.

  6. Validate Azure subscription and purchasing requirements. Confirm that the subscription is eligible and that your organization permits the required Azure Marketplace or Security Store provider purchase.

  7. Estimate costs. Review provider pricing and expected Azure infrastructure charges before deployment.

Learn more

  • Supported telecommunications providers and provider offers

  • Azure resource requirements and pricing guidance

Title: Generally Available: Azure Cosmos DB Safe Key Rotation

Body.Content:
Safe Key Rotation for Azure Cosmos DB is now generally available. You can view timestamp metadata showing when each account key was last used, helping you identify active keys before rotating or retiring credentials.

This visibility helps reduce the risk of service disruptions caused by disabling keys that are still in use. It also gives you actionable insights to improve credential management, maintain application continuity, and support modern security and compliance practices.

Title: Public Preview: Disable VNet peering route

Body.Content:
Announcing the public preview of disable VNet peering route, a route-table capability that gives you more control over traffic between peered virtual networks. DPR suppresses system-generated peering routes on subnets associated with the route table while preserving the peering connection itself.     

In large hub-and-spoke networks, you can pair this feature with a summarized user-defined route to direct traffic through a network virtual appliance, such as Azure Firewall, instead of maintaining a separate override for every spoke. This helps simplify route management as your network grows.            

Manage DPR through route-table configuration or Azure Virtual Network Manager routing rule collections. You configure the replacement UDRs and inspection path; DPR does not create them automatically.        

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Service tag match condition for Azure Front Door Premium WAF

Body.Content:
Announcing the general availability of the service tag match condition for Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) custom rules on Azure Front Door Premium. 

Service tags represent groups of IP address prefixes used by Azure services, and Microsoft updates them automatically as addresses change. Custom rules can now match a HTTP request's source IP address against service tags, so you can control traffic from Azure services without building and maintaining lists of IPs.  

With service tag matching, you can: 

  • Allow Azure services your application relies on, such as monitoring and health checks, through to your endpoints. 
  • Block traffic from Azure services your application never expects to receive requests from. 
  • Restrict sensitive paths, such as admin endpoints, by combining a service tag with URI, host, or request method conditions. 
  • Rate limit traffic from an Azure service instead of blocking it outright. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Keyless TLS on Application Gateway with Azure Key Vault Managed HSM

Body.Content:
Azure Application Gateway now supports keyless TLS termination using certificates whose private keys stay in Azure Key Vault Managed HSM. Each TLS handshake signature is performed inside the HSM, and the private key is never exported to the gateway. 

This integration helps you: 

  • Maintain private key custody within a dedicated HSM boundary. 
  • Use managed identities and role-based access control for key access. 
  • Monitor signing operations through Managed HSM diagnostic logs. 
  • Obtain cryptographic evidence that the TLS key was generated and is stored in a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSM. 
  • Support separation of duties and centralized key management. 

Learn more: 

  • What is keyless TLS for Azure Application Gateway and Azure Key Vault Managed HSM? 
  • Tutorial: Configure keyless TLS termination with Azure Key Vault Managed HSM 
  • What is Azure Key Vault Managed HSM?

Title: Generally Available: Azure DNS enables DNS-based load balancing through Traffic Manager linked records

Body.Content:
Azure DNS now provides DNS based load balancing by seamless integration with Azure Traffic Manager. Customers can directly associate an Azure DNS record set with a Traffic Manager profile, eliminating the need to create a CNAME record pointing to the trafficmanager.net domain. 

This integration reduces DNS lookup latency by removing the additional CNAME lookup and enables DNSSEC compatibility for load-balanced records by removing the unsigned trafficmanager.net domain from the DNS resolution chain.

Title: Public Preview: Azure Databricks Private network gateway

Body.Content:
Private network gateway for Azure Databricks is now in Public Preview, enabling serverless compute to connect to resources in your virtual network (VNet) and transitively connected networks through a single managed gateway. Customers can use the gateway to access multiple private resources, route serverless egress through their own firewalls or network security appliances, and use stable, identifiable source IP addresses. 

This simplifies secure connectivity for serverless workloads while giving organizations greater control over network traffic and access to private resources. 

Private network gateway integrates with existing network connectivity configurations (NCCs) and complements Azure Private Link, providing additional flexibility for securing serverless network connectivity. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: External key management for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM

Body.Content:
External key management for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM is now generally available in all Azure public regions. For organizations with regulatory or sovereignty requirements to retain physical control of key-encryption keys, it lets Azure services that support customer-managed keys with Managed HSM use keys held in a customer-operated hardware security module (HSM) outside Microsoft infrastructure. Managed HSM delegates key wrap and unwrap operations through a customer-operated proxy; the external key material stays outside Microsoft infrastructure.

Access requires enablement through your Microsoft account team. Connectivity to the proxy over the public internet is available with the GA feature. Azure Private Link integration is in public preview. Customers or their HSM providers are responsible for the external HSM, proxy, and network availability; these components are outside the Managed HSM service-level agreement (SLA).

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Standard service endpoint

Body.Content:
Standard service endpoint, a new capability in the Azure Private Link family, provides a scalable and secure approach for connecting Azure IaaS workloads to Azure PaaS services. Standard service endpoint addresses the manageability, and the scale limitations of traditional service endpoints by using Public IP addresses as network identifiers and integrating with network security perimeter. This enables organizations to achieve large-scale IaaS-to-PaaS connectivity while maintaining strong network access controls and simplified operations. 

With standard service endpoint, customers can associate a public IP instance with multiple subnets and virtual networks across subscriptions within the same tenant and region. When combined with network security perimeter, organizations can create a logical security boundary around supported Azure services, including Azure Storage, Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB, and Azure Key Vault. Access can then be restricted so that only approved networks and workloads are allowed to communicate with these resources, helping reduce operational complexity while strengthening security posture. 

Standard service endpoint is a paid Azure feature and is billed at a fixed rate per virtual network (VNet) per hour. 

Learn more: 

  • Documentation  
  • Azure Private Link pricing

Title: Generally Availabile: Automatic zone balance for Virtual Machine Scale Sets

Body.Content:
Automatic zone balance for Virtual Machine Scale Sets is now generally available. This feature continuously monitors scale sets deployed across availability zones and automatically redistributes VM instances when zonal imbalances occur. This helps reduce the risk that a single-zone outage disproportionately affects an application.

Automatic zone balance uses a create-before-delete approach: Azure creates a replacement VM in an under-provisioned zone and validates its health before removing an instance from an over-provisioned zone. Built-in safeguards respect instance protection policies, coordinate with Azure Autoscale, avoid active or recently completed scale-set operations, apply cooldown periods, and replace only one VM at a time. 

This capability is best suited for stateless workloads and requires at least two availability zones, zonal instances, and application health monitoring. It can be enabled through the Azure portal, Azure CLI, PowerShell, or REST API.

Learn more.

Title: Retirement: Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc enabled Kubernetes clusters

Body.Content:
The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on October 9, 2027.

Customers currently using the extension should plan to migrate to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension before the retirement date. The Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension provides equivalent functionality for accessing and synchronizing secrets from Azure Key Vault for workloads running on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. In addition, the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension includes enhancements such as support for offline access to secrets and authentication using workload identity federation, enabling applications to access Azure Key Vault without storing long-lived credentials on the cluster.

After retirement, the Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support.

Migration guidance is available to help customers transition their workloads and configurations to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension ahead of retirement.

Title: Retirement: Microsoft Dev Box will be retired on September 18, 2028

Body.Content:
Microsoft Dev Box will retire on September 18, 2028. Beginning on September 14, 2026, Microsoft Dev Box will begin the closing-down process. After retirement, Microsoft Dev Box will no longer be available. 

Microsoft Dev Box is currently in maintenance mode, and Microsoft’s investments for developer cloud environments are focused on Windows 365. Existing Microsoft Dev Box usage remains supported during the transition period, and we recommend that you begin planning your migration now to avoid disruption to developer workflows. 

What this means for you 

  • If you currently use Microsoft Dev Box, you can continue using your existing deployments during the transition period. 
  • No new feature development is planned for the service. 
  • You should evaluate and begin planning your move to Windows 365, which is the recommended path forward for virtualized developer environments. 

Recommended action 

  • Review your current Dev Box usage, including dev centers, projects, pools, images, and developer workflows. 
  • Identify which scenarios can transition directly to Windows 365 and which require additional planning. 
  • Validate identity, device management, networking, image, and licensing requirements for your future-state environment. 
  • Begin testing replacement workflows as early as possible to reduce risk before retirement.  

If you have questions or need support, please contact your Microsoft representative.

Title: Retirement: Azure Deployment Environments will be retired on February 22, 2027

Body.Content:
Azure Deployment Environments will retire on February 22, 2027. Beginning on September 14, 2026, Azure Deployment Environments will begin the closing-down process. After retirement, the service will no longer be available. 

To help avoid disruption, we recommend that you begin assessing your current usage and planning your transition now. Review the environments, templates, and workflows in your organization that depend on Azure Deployment Environments and identify the replacement approach that best supports your requirements. 

What this means for you 

  • You should review all current Azure Deployment Environments usage across subscriptions, projects, templates, and deployment workflows. 
  • You should identify an alternative approach for environment provisioning and developer self-service before the retirement date. 
  • You should begin validating your migration plan as early as possible to minimize operational and development impact. 

Recommended action 

  • Inventory your current environments, templates, catalogs, and provisioning workflows. 
  • Determine the target platform or service that will replace Azure Deployment Environments for your organization. 
  • Test your migration path, including governance, access control, infrastructure-as-code compatibility, and developer workflow readiness. 
  • Communicate internal timelines to platform engineering teams, developers, and administrators.

Title: Generally Available: Exceptions in WAF for Azure Application Gateway and Azure Front Door

Body.Content:
Announcing the general availability of exceptions for Web Application Firewall on Azure Application Gateway and Azure Front Door.

Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) helps protect your web applications from common threats and attacks. In some cases, WAF may block requests that are safe and expected for your application. Existing exclusions help reduce false positives by omitting specific request attributes, such as headers, cookies, query string arguments, or body fields, from WAF evaluation while the rest of the request continues to be inspected. 

Exceptions provide additional flexibility by allowing specific requests to bypass WAF inspection at the rule, rule group, or managed ruleset level. Exceptions can be defined using request URI, remote IP address, or request header name and value, helping customers tune WAF policies more precisely while keeping other protections active. 

To configure exceptions, navigate to your WAF policy in the Azure portal, select Managed rules, and then add an exception. 

Learn more: 

  • Application Gateway documentation 
  • Front Door documentation

Title: Public Preview: Microsoft Agent 365 integration with Azure API Management

Body.Content:
The integration between Microsoft Agent 365 and Azure API Management is now available in public preview, helping organizations connect centralized governance with runtime enforcement for MCP servers and tools.

With this integration, organizations can:

  • Discover Azure API Management gateways and MCP servers in Agent 365, creating a centralized inventory of gateway-managed tools.

  • Control access to MCP servers from Agent 365, with enforcement applied by Azure API Management at runtime.

  • Apply tool-level access controls with the Azure API Management AI Gateway tier, including blocking individual tools without disabling the entire MCP server.

  • Monitor tool activity to support auditing, operational visibility, and incident investigation.

  • Protect tool interactions using Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview capabilities to evaluate tool requests and responses for security threats and sensitive-information risks.

Azure API Management v2 tiers support centralized MCP inventory and server-level blocking and unblocking. The AI Gateway tier, currently in preview, adds individual tool-level blocking, tool activity observability, and tool threat protection.

This integration enables AI administrators to manage governance centrally in Agent 365 while platform teams enforce those policies through Azure API Management in the customer’s Azure environment.

Title: Generally Available: Anyscale on Azure

Body.Content: Anyscale on Azure is now Generally Available. Anyscale on Azure is a managed platform for running distributed Python workloads on Ray. It deploys directly onto your Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster and integrates with the Azure services your team already uses. Unlike other processing engines which either only support one hardware type (e.g. CPUs) or focus on a single workload (e.g. inference), Ray turns a heterogeneous cluster of CPUs and GPUs into a single Python runtime composing data preparation, distributed training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, high-throughput inference, and agentic execution as one program. Anyscale on Azure brings Ray, the distributed compute runtime,  into your Azure tenant as an Azure Native service, that includes purpose-built developer tooling and unified pane for cluster management, built through deep engineering collaboration between Anyscale and Microsoft.

Title: Generally Available: Enabling the Bulk admin role for SQL Server on Linux

Body.Content:
Starting with SQL Server 2025 CU9 and SQL Server 2022 CU27, SQL Server on Linux supports the bulkadmin fixed server role and the ADMINISTER BULK OPERATIONS permission for performing bulk data import operations without requiring users to be members of the sysadmin fixed server role. 

This capability enables you to use operations such as BULK INSERT and OPENROWSET(BULK...) while following a least-privilege security model. Previously on SQL Server on Linux, these operations required sysadmin membership.

With this release, organizations running SQL Server on Linux can provide users with the permissions required for bulk data loading without granting broader sysadmin privileges, improving alignment with the principle of least privilege. The feature applies to SQL Server on Linux, including on-premises, SQL Server on Azure VMs and container deployments.

Learn more.

Title: Retirement: Pod name dimension in AKS pod platform metrics

Body.Content:
Beginning September 30, 2027, support for the pod name dimension on the following Azure Monitor platform metrics is retiring, and these metrics are transitioning to aggregate pod counters:
  • Number of pods by phase (kube_pod_status_phase)
  • Number of pods in Ready state (kube_pod_status_ready)
After this change:
  • Metric names remain unchanged.
  • Aggregate pod counts remain available.
  • Namespace-level monitoring scenarios remain supported.
  • The pod name dimension will no longer be available for filtering, grouping, or alerting.
During the deprecation period, AKS will maintain both the existing and the new aggregate implementations. Both are populated with data, existing monitoring experiences will continue to function, and you will have at least one year of historical data in the aggregate implementation before retirement.
You may be affected if any dashboard, workbook, alert, automation, or monitoring workflow:
  • Uses kube_pod_status_phase or kube_pod_status_ready and filters on the pod name dimension.
  • Splits or groups results by the pod name dimension.
Recommended action:
  • If you use aggregate pod counts, no action is required.
  • If you use the pod name dimension, update dashboards, alerts, workbooks, and automation before September 30, 2027. For pod-level monitoring and troubleshooting, we recommend using Azure Monitor Managed Prometheus and Kubernetes-native pod metrics.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

Title: Retirement: Azure App Service on Azure Stack Hub

Body.Content:
Azure App Service on Azure Stack Hub will be retired on September 30, 2029. 

Starting September 30, 2026, new installations will no longer be supported, and no new product releases, features, or enhancements will be made available. Existing supported deployments can continue to run and upgrade to the latest available release until retirement. 

Customers should begin planning migration to Azure App Service in Azure now to continue receiving support, security updates, platform improvements, and new capabilities. 

On September 30th, 2029, App Service on Azure Stack will reach retirement and Microsoft support will end. 

Recommended action  

Assessand migrate applications as soon as possible. Azure App Service in Azure provides a fully managed platform with global availability, Windows and Linux hosting options, autoscale, deployment slots, advanced networking and security, Azure services integration, and continuous innovation. 

For applications with complex Windows dependencies, evaluate Managed Instance on Azure App Service. It can help accelerate migration for applications requiring registry access, COM components, custom runtimes, or other Windows-specific dependencies. 

For a successful transition, inventory applications and dependencies, assess compatibility, select the appropriate Azure hosting target, migrate code, configuration, and data, validate workloads, and complete migration before September 30, 2029. 

Learn more:  

  • Benefits 
  • Plan 
  • Migrate

Title: Retirement: Always Encrypted with Intel SGX Enclaves

Body.Content:
Always Encrypted with Intel SGX enclaves in Azure SQL Database will retire on October 31, 2027 as support for SGX-enabled DC-series hardware is phased out. Customers should transition to Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) enclaves, a hardware-independent alternative, or consider SQL Server on Confidential VMs.

Customer impact

After retirement, workloads using Intel SGX enclaves will no longer have enclave functionality. Databases running on DC-series compute tiers should be migrated to supported compute tiers to continue using enclave-enabled features.

Recommended actions

  • Migrate from DC-series to a supported Standard-series (non-DC) compute tier.
  • Enable VBS enclaves for Always Encrypted. No attestation is required.
  • Update client drivers to versions that support VBS enclaves.
  • Update connection strings to remove SGX attestation parameters and use VBS enclave mode.
We recommend planning and validating your migration well in advance of the retirement date to ensure a smooth transition.

Title: Public Preview: AKS on bare metal now on Ubuntu

Body.Content:
Running Kubernetes on-premises often means adding a virtualization layer, adapting to unfamiliar infrastructure, or giving up control over the hardware and software your applications depend on. For AI workloads, these tradeoffs can limit access to local data, reduce available compute capacity, and restrict your choice of GPUs, drivers, and runtimes.

AKS on bare metal Ubuntu, now in public preview, brings the AKS experience directly to customer owned Ubuntu infrastructure. Deploy a complete Kubernetes cluster on your hardware using Azure CLI. Choose the CPU and GPU hardware and supporting software stack that fit your workloads.

Run applications close to your data, dedicate more infrastructure capacity to your workloads, and manage Kubernetes through familiar AKS and Azure workflows. You keep the flexibility of Ubuntu and your hardware while extending a consistent AKS operating model to your on-premises environment.

Learn more.

Title: Announcing: Table discovery in OneLake Catalog search

Body.Content:
Starting October 15, 2026, Search in Microsoft Fabric will return tables from semantic models, lakehouses, and mirrored databases as individual results. Users can search by table name or description, or find a table by an exact column-name match.  More object types will become available over time. This applies to Fabric's global search, the OneLake Catalog UI, the Search API, search in Fabric's MCP servers, the /find command in the Fabric CLI, and the discovery skill.

What you need to know: 
Table visibility in search follows permissions on the parent item, not data-level permissions on the table. If a user has Read permission or higher on the item, they can discover all tables under that item, even tables they can't query. 

Search does not grant access to table data; existing data-access controls still apply when a user opens or queries a table. Tables in semantic models protected by object-level security are excluded from search. 

Action: 
Review "Users can find objects in search" setting in the Fabric admin portal under Tenant settings. It's enabled by default. Turn it off if your organization isn't ready for users to find tables by search; item and data access won't change.

Title: Public Preview: Azure Backup for PostgreSQL flexible server and elastic cluster (v2)

Body.Content:
Azure Backup for PostgreSQL flexible server and elastic cluster (v2) preview brings enterprise-grade long-term retention to PostgreSQL. Backups are taken as physical backups from managed disk snapshots and vaulted in an Azure Backup vault, so protection now extends to servers of up to 32 TB on Premium SSD v1 and up to 64 TB on Premium SSD v2. The first backup is full and every backup after it is incremental, which keeps daily protection practical at multi-terabyte scale, with a recovery point objective goal of one day and retention configurable from 7 days up to 10 years.

The v1 solution took logical backups, which capped server size at 1 TB, allowed a single vaulted backup each week, produced full copies every time, and returned data as files that had to be imported by hand before it could be used. Physical backups lift those constraints together, extend protection to elastic cluster as well as flexible server, and introduce Restore as Server.

The preview includes the following capabilities:
  • Backup for both PostgreSQL flexible server and elastic cluster.
  • Servers of up to 32 TB on Premium SSD v1 and up to 64 TB on Premium SSD v2.
  • Daily and weekly schedules, along with on-demand backups.
  • Incremental backups after the first full backup, with a recovery point objective goal of one day.
  • Restore as Server onto a pre-created flexible server or elastic cluster, with no intermediate storage account and no manual import.
  • Retention up to 10 years with independent daily, weekly, monthly and yearly rules, protected by vault soft delete, immutability, Multi-user authorization and Customer Managed Key encryption.
  • Support for WORM immutable backups, so that recovery points cannot be altered or deleted before their retention period expires.
Billing will be enabled from October 15, 2026.  

Learn more: 

  • Documentation   
  • Azure Backup pricing 
  • Pricing calculator

Title: Public Preview: IPv6 Support for Application Gateway WAF

Body.Content:
Announcing the Public Preview of IPv6 support for Application Gateway WAF.

Application Gateway Web Application Firewall (WAF) now supports inspection and enforcement for IPv6 traffic in Public Preview, marking a major step forward in modernizing the platform for dual‑stack environments. As IPv6 adoption accelerates globally due to IPv4 exhaustion and modern connectivity requirements, this enhancement enables customers to embrace IPv6 without compromising their security posture.

With this update, Application Gateway WAF extends its full protection stack -including managed rule sets, custom rules, and diagnostics - to IPv6 traffic. Customers operating dual‑stack applications can now apply consistent security controls across both IPv4 and IPv6. Additionally, IPv6 geo‑based custom rules are available through AFEC enrollment, providing more granular traffic governance during the preview.

Learn more.

Title: Public Preview: Major version upgrades (MVU) for Azure Database for PostgreSQL elastic clusters

Body.Content:
MVUs are now available for elastic clusters in Azure Database for PostgreSQL. You can upgrade an existing elastic cluster to a supported newer PostgreSQL version in place without provisioning a replacement cluster, migrating distributed data, or changing your application connection endpoint. This managed upgrade experience helps reduce the downtime, complexity, and operational effort associated with traditional migration-based upgrades.

For technical questions, issues, and help get answers in Microsoft Q&A.

Title: Retirement: Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 Azure VMs

Body.Content:
As part of the Microsoft Azure VM lifecycle policy, Microsoft is announcing the retirement of the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 Azure VM series in public cloud Azure regions. These VMs will enter the End-of-Life lifecycle stage and retire on November 15, 2029. 

We know migrating production workloads takes planning and engineering time. To keep your applications and workloads running without interruption, migrate any Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, or Esv3 series VMs to a newer VM series before November 15, 2029. After this date, Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 virtual machines will enter the Retired lifecycle stage and will no longer be supported on Azure. Virtual machines not transitioned by that time may be deallocated and ultimately deleted as the underlying hardware and platform infrastructure are retired. We recommend evaluating available modernization options as soon as possible and moving to newer VM generations, such as Azure Dsv5 or Esv5v5 series virtual machines, to maintain uninterrupted service and gain improved performance, security, and reliability.  

Additionally, as previously communicated, as of July 1, 2026, one-year and three-year Reserved Instances (RIs) for the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 VM series are no longer available for purchase or renewal. If you would like to continue commitment savings, we recommend reviewing your current reserved instance orders and if RIs are still in effect for these VMs, consider a trade-in of active reservations for Azure savings plan for compute contracts.   

Help and support   

Microsoft is committed to ensuring every customer navigates this transition quickly, successfully, and with clarity. Customers with an active support plan can submit a support request for technical assistance with migration planning and execution. For general questions, Microsoft Q&A provides access to community experts.  

Learn more:   

  • Azure Virtual Machines Lifecycle policy  
  • v5 modernization guide   
  • Modernize to the v6 and v7 VM series - Azure Virtual Machines

Title: Retirement: Functions on Azure Container Apps V1

Body.Content:
The Functions on Azure Container Apps (ACA) V1 will be retired on September 29, 2027. After this date, existing Functions on ACA V1 Apps will stop running and no longer process requests or event-driven triggers. 

Action required 

Review your Azure environments and migrate all affected apps to the Functions on Azure Container Apps(ACA) V2 hosting model before September 29, 2027 to avoid service disruption. 

Functions on ACA V2 uses a native Azure Container App configured with `kind=functionapp`. You can reuse your existing container image; the standard migration path doesn't require function code changes. 

Use the Azure Functions on Azure Container Apps v1 migration assistant to help migrate your function apps from the V1 to V2 model. 

To migrate manually 

1. Record the V1 app's configuration, including secrets, identity, networking, and scaling. 

2. Create a V2 app with `kind=functionapp` and reapply the configuration. 

3. Test all triggers, shift production traffic, and then decommission the V1 app. 

We recommend completing migration and production validation well before the retirement date. 

For assistance, contact your Microsoft account team or create an Azure support request.  

Learn more: 

  • Migrate to Azure Functions v2 on Azure Container Apps 
  • Create an Azure Functions app with auto scaling rules on Azure Container Apps

Title: Generally Available: Storage optimized Lasv5 and Laosv5 Azure VM series

Body.Content:
The Laosv5 series and Lasv5 storage optimized VMs, based on the 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ processor (Turin), are now generally available.

Lasv5 and Laosv5 VMs have sizes ranging from 2-160 vCPUs, with 8GiB of memory and 720GB of local NVMe disk capacity per vCPU.  Both support 200Gbps of network bandwidth and deliver up to 35% better average CPU performance. The Lasv5 VMs offer up to 30.7TB of local storage capacity with 9.6M read IOPS performance, while the Laosv5 VMs offer up to 138TB of local storage capacity with 20.7M read IOPS performance.

These VM series are powered by Azure Boost and Azure Boost SSDs, enable NVMe local SSD disk encryption by default, and come with an NVMe remote storage interface with support for premium storage caching, significantly improving remote storage performance.

Compared to the previous generation Lasv4 VMs, Lasv5 VMs have:

  • 33% larger maximum local storage capacity

  • 9% larger temp disk random read IOPS per vCPU

  • New 128 and 160 vCPU sizes

Compared to the previous generation Laosv4 VMs, Laosv5 VMs have:

  • 500% larger maximum local storage capacity

  • 619% larger maximum read IOPS

  • New 48, 64, 96, 128, and160 vCPU sizes

All L-series v5 VMs are perfect for distributed, scale-out workloads that require high amounts of local storage capacity per vCPU and the ability to move that data quickly over the network or to an Azure remote storage backend.

Learn more.

Title: Public Preview: Automatic Zone Placement for Virtual Machine Scale Sets

Body.Content:
Automatic Zone Placement for VM Scale Sets (Public Preview) enables Azure to automatically select the best availability zones for your scale set based on SKU availability, capacity, and placement requirements. Instead of manually maintaining zone lists for each region, customers can use a consistent configuration across regions while Azure handles zone selection.

Key benefits include:

  • Simplified multi-region deployments with no region-specific zone management.
  • Capacity-aware zone selection to improve deployment and scale-out success.
  • Flexible resiliency controls that let you define zone spread and per-zone capacity limits.
  • Greater allocation flexibility by allowing Azure to use additional eligible zones when needed.
  • Support for both new and existing VM Scale Sets using Uniform or Flexible orchestration modes.

By default, Automatic Zone Placement distributes instances evenly across three availability zones, maintains a minimum spread across two zones, limits any single zone to 50% of total instances, and can expand into additional zones if required for scaling. Customers can further customize eligible zones, zone count, balancing behavior, and capacity distribution to meet workload needs.

The feature only affects placement of new VM instances and does not rebalance existing VMs. Existing deployments can use Automatic Zone Balance to correct zone imbalances.

Automatic Zone Placement is available in public preview through the Azure portal, CLI, PowerShell, and REST API. To get started, register the Microsoft.Compute/VmssAutomaticZonePlacement AFEC, use Compute API version March 1, 2026 or later, and configure a VM Scale Set with the Auto zone placement policy.

Title: Generally Available: Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server supports cross-tenant customer-managed keys (CMK)

Body.Content:
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server now supports cross-tenant customer-managed keys (CMK). You can encrypt your data using keys stored in an Azure Key Vault or Azure Managed HSM that resides in a different Microsoft Entra tenant than your PostgreSQL server. This update is ideal for SaaS providers and ISVs that need to keep database operations and key ownership in separate tenants. 

With cross-tenant CMK, you can keep full control of your encryption keys while applications and databases run in a service provider's tenant. This separation helps you meet security and compliance requirements by keeping key management independent from service operations, while allowing you to manage key rotation and revocation on your terms. 

Learn more

Title: Generally Available: SQL Server on Azure Local Disconnected (ALDO)

Body.Content:
Now you can use ALDO to extend SQL Server support to environments that can’t maintain continuous connectivity to Azure. ALDO is designed for operations in highly regulated, secure, remote, or air-gapped environments, where internet connectivity is restricted or unavailable. SQL Server workloads continue to run entirely on Azure Local infrastructure while maintaining operational independence from cloud connectivity. 

In addition to traditional database workloads, you can use ALDO to support local AI and intelligent application scenarios in disconnected environments. By keeping data, AI models, and SQL Server workloads within the same secure infrastructure boundary, you can build and run AI-powered solutions without requiring cloud connectivity. This is particularly valuable for defense, government, manufacturing, energy, and remote-edge deployments where data sovereignty, security, and operational continuity are critical requirements. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Database DevOps in SSMS powered by SQL projects

Body.Content:
In SSMS, you can now use Microsoft.Build.Sql projects to help you implement, manage, and collaborate on database changes, by providing a local definition of the database objects. Title: Public Preview: Azure SQL Database Hyperscale Serverless auto-pause and auto-resume

Body.Content:
Auto-pause and auto-resume are now available in public preview for Azure SQL Hyperscale databases using the Serverless compute tier. You can configure databases to automatically pause during periods of inactivity and automatically resume when activity returns, helping reduce costs for workloads that experience extended or predictable idle periods.  

When a database is paused, compute billing stops and only storage-related charges continue to apply. Auto-pause and auto-resume can be enabled for both new and existing Azure SQL Hyperscale databases using the Serverless compute tier.  

Learn more.

Title: Retirement: Azure Arc enabled System Center Virtual Machine Manager will be retired September 30, 2029

Body.Content:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Arc-enabled System Center Virtual Machine Manager (SCVMM) in September 2029. Customers must plan and transition to alternative solutions.

What does this mean for you?

If you are using Azure Arc-enabled SCVMM for:
  • Azure services and Azure Arc capabilities such as monitoring, security, governance, updates, and licensing for Extended Security Updates and Pay-as-you-go SQL and WS, we recommend switching to Azure Arc-enabled Servers.
  • VM lifecycle and powercycle operations such as create, start, stop, restart, resize, and self-service VM management, we recommend that you reach out to us through e-mail to arc-vmm-feedback@microsoft.com.
What action should you take?
  1. Review your current use of Azure Arc-enabled SCVMM.
  2. Determine the appropriate migration path: Azure Arc-enabled Servers or if you need help, reach out to Microsoft.
  3. Follow the migration guidance to deboard your SCVMM environment from Azure Arc and onboard to your alternative solution.
We recommend beginning your transition planning as soon as possible to ensure a smooth migration before retirement. You can also share your feedback or any concerns that you may have during this transition through e-mail to arc-vmm-feedback@microsoft.com.

Learn more.

Title: Public Preview: Migrate directly from Azure Arc to Azure SQL Database, including Hyperscale

Body.Content:
You can now select Azure SQL Database, including Hyperscale, as a migration target directly from the database migration experience in Azure Arc. The workflow brings Azure Database Migration Service and Self-hosted Integration Runtime setup into the guided portal journey, allowing you to assess your SQL Server estate, choose your target, configure your migration and monitor progress without leaving Arc.

Until now, your path from assessment to migration required stepping outside Arc, learning a separate service, configuring a runtime, and moving between multiple tools. This additional effort slowed modernization projects. With this release, the databases Arc already identified as migration-ready become databases you can act on immediately, in the same place you assessed them.

You get the same migration dashboard, monitoring experience, and guided workflow already used for other Azure SQL destinations, so choosing Hyperscale does not require learning a new migration methodology. Runtime setup is guided and completed only once, with in-portal instructions that walk you through the process.

Learn more.

Title: Retirement: Microsoft HPC Pack

Body.Content:
Microsoft is retiring all versions of HPC Pack. End of Support is August 27, 2027. HPC Pack is now entering a one-year retirement period. Microsoft will provide limited, retirement-only support during this period. The scope of this support is defined below so customers know what to expect. 

In scope until End of Support: 

• Security/CVE response and necessary security updates. 

• Guidance from existing documentation and validated configurations. 

• Assistance with supported components and documented functionality. 

• Case-by-case evaluation of long-term support options where available. 

Out of scope: 

• Non-security fixes or product improvements. 

• New features, custom code, or design changes. 

• Validation of new operating systems, hardware, dependencies, architectures, or integrations. 

• New product investigation or documentation. 

• Migration planning, execution, or consulting. 

• Unsupported configurations. 

After August 27, 2027, HPC Pack will receive no updates, fixes, or technical support. Existing deployments will remain operational but unsupported. 

Required action 

Begin assessing and transitioning workloads now. Consider Azure Batch for managed parallel and HPC scheduling, or another appropriate Azure service. No alternative guarantees one-to-one feature parity. Engage your Microsoft account team or Cloud Solution Architect for planning. 

Share customer needs and transition challenges through this form: ESU Extend Request.

Title: Retirement: Azure IoT Central will be retired on September 20, 2029

Body.Content:
Azure IoT Central will be retired on September 20, 2029. You can continue using Azure IoT Central until the retirement date, but we recommend starting your transition planning early.

Why is this happening?

As Azure IoT evolves, Microsoft is focusing future investment on Azure IoT platform services that provide greater scalability, architectural flexibility, lifecycle management, and integration with Microsoft Fabric for analytics and AI-driven workloads. Azure IoT Hub, Device Provisioning Service (DPS), and Azure Device Registry represent the recommended Azure-native platform for connected operations.

Recommended action 

  • Review your current Azure IoT Central applications, devices, dashboards, , and integrations.
  • Evaluate Azure IoT Hub and DPS as the target architecture for device connectivity and provisioning.
  • Evaluate Microsoft Fabric for real-time analytics, dashboards, and broader data experiences.
  • Use the Azure IoT Central migration playbook to map existing IoT Central scenarios to Azure IoT services. 
  • Begin planning and executing your transition before September 20, 2029. 
  • If additional assistance is required, engage Microsoft field teams or an Azure IoT migration partner. 

Help and support 

If you have questions, get answers from community experts through Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical assistance, create an Azure support request.

Title: Generally Available: Support for large volume breakthrough mode

Body.Markdown:
Large volume breakthrough mode in Azure NetApp Files enables extreme performance and scalability for demanding HPC and EDA workloads. It supports large volumes up to 2PiB, delivering throughput up to 80 GiBps, depending on workload characteristics. Large volume breakthrough mode uses six storage endpoints for each large volume ensuring consistent performance. Storage systems hosting breakthrough mode volumes are reserved for each customer to provide peak performance and not compete with other workloads. Key benefits include:

High-capacity scaling for large-scale, latency-sensitive workloads

Simplified network management with multiple storage endpoints per volume

Dedicated capacity stamps to eliminate noisy neighbor interference and maintain predictable performance

Supported in all regions where dedicated capacity has been ordered and provisioned for the customer.

How to create a volume with large volume breakthrough mode enabled:

Create a NFS volume

Create a SMB volume

Create a dual protocol volume

Body.Content:
Vector search and vector indexes are now generally available in Azure SQL Database. Using the CREATE VECTOR INDEX and VECTOR_SEARCH T-SQL capabilities, you can perform efficient approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches for AI scenarios such as semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), recommendation systems, and image search. Built on the DiskANN algorithm, vector indexes enable efficient vector similarity search over large datasets while allowing you to combine vector search with relational queries and filtering directly in Azure SQL Database. 

By bringing AI retrieval directly into Azure SQL Database, you can build AI-powered applications on your enterprise data without requiring a separate vector database, simplifying application architecture while leveraging the reliability, security, and governance capabilities of Azure SQL Database. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Azure Backup for Elastic SAN

Body.Content:
Azure Backup now supports operational backup for Elastic SAN, offering a fully managed solution for backing up and restoring Elastic SAN volumes. This integration helps protect data against accidental deletions, ransomware attacks, and application updates by exporting Elastic SAN volumes to independent Managed Disk Incremental Snapshots. These snapshots are stored in locally redundant storage and are independent of the Elastic SAN volume lifecycle. 

The solution supports up to 450 restore points with 24 hours backup frequency. It is generally available in all Azure regions and supports volumes up to 16 TiB. Long-term vaulted backups and hourly backups are not supported. 

Standard charges apply for Managed Disk Incremental Snapshots.

To get started, visit the Resiliency center and configure protection for your Elastic SAN volumes. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Instant Access for VM restore points

Body.Content:
Instant Access for application-consistent restore points on virtual machines (that have Premium v2 or Ultra disks as data disks) is now generally available. With Instant Access, you can begin restoring a disk from a restore point as soon as the snapshot is created, instead of waiting for the background data replication to complete fully. That shortens your recovery time objective when you are bringing a VM back online.

What's new at general availability

This release introduces “instantAccessState”, a consolidated read-only property on the restore point itself. During preview, customer had to inspect “snapshotAccessState” on each individual disk restore point and work out for themselves whether the restore point as a whole was usable. Now the customer can read one property at the restore point level and decide in a single step whether they can restore, copy, or download it, which removes per-disk polling logic from recovery automation and makes restore decision much simpler.

How to use it

Set instantAccess to true on the restore point collection to enable Instant Access for every restore point in it and optionally set instantAccessDurationMinutes on the restore point to control how long Instant Access stays active (60–300 minutes; the default is 300). Before you trigger a restore, read instantAccessState on the restore point and decide to restore based on its value rather than aggregating per-disk states yourself. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Azure Container Apps Sandboxes

Body.Content:
Teams building agentic applications, multi-tenant platforms, development environments, and CI/CD systems have often had to stitch together custom infrastructure to run untrusted code safely, preserve state across sessions, and handle bursty demand without paying for idle capacity. Azure Container Apps Sandboxes addresses that challenge with a new first-class resource type in Azure Container Apps that provides fast, secure, ephemeral compute environments with built-in suspend and resume capabilities. 

Each sandbox runs in its own hardware-isolated microVM boundary, supports standard OCI container images, and starts in sub-second time. It can preserve memory, disk state, and preloaded libraries in a snapshot, so workloads resume quickly from the same point without incurring a cold start reload penalty. For technical practitioners, this means they can now run AI-generated or otherwise untrusted workloads in strongly isolated environments, preserve execution context across long-running tasks, and scale from zero to thousands of concurrent sandboxes using the same Azure foundation that also powers offerings such as GitHub Sandbox, hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service, and Azure Container Apps Express. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Azure Container Apps Express

Body.Content:
Azure Container Apps Express is now generally available. It is the simplest and fastest way to launch and scale powerful applications on Azure, from zero to hyperscale, without infrastructure decisions. It represents the first Azure compute platform purpose-built for agent and developer use alike. 

Express is based on years of experience running Azure Container Apps at a large scale. We have learned that most developers working on web apps, APIs and agents want to deploy quickly, have automatic scaling, and avoid dealing with complex infrastructure. Express provides these features. It sets up your environment in seconds, can handle any amount of traffic, and removes complicated settings. This helps teams move from writing code to having a production-ready app in just minutes, not hours. 

Express is purpose-built for workloads serving developers and agents alike. It provides opinionated, production-grade defaults: autoscaling, per-second billing, managed identity, secrets management, custom domains, container registry integration, revision management, and built-in observability. Just bring your container, Azure Container Apps Express handles everything else. 

Learn more.

Title: Retirement: Support for .NET 8 and .NET 9 ends on November 10, 2026—upgrade your apps to .NET 10

Body.Content:
Support for .NET 8 and .NET 9 will end on November 10, 2026. Please transition to .NET 10 by that date. Your Azure Function Apps will continue to operate, but security updates will no longer be provided, and support for .NET 8 and .NET 9 on Azure Functions will end. Running Function Apps on an unsupported runtime or language version might lead to security and performance issues. 

Upgrade to .NET 10 before November 10, 2026 to remain on a supported version. Learn more about Azure Functions stack version support. 

Required action  

To avoid potential security vulnerabilities, minimize risk for your Azure Functions apps, and take advantage of latest features, you must take action based on your current configuration: 

If your app is using the in-process model: 
Migrate your app to the isolated worker model, then upgrade to .NET 10. For guidance, see: 

  • Migrate C# Apps from In-Process to Isolated Worker Model 
  • Update Language Versions in Azure Functions 

If your app is already using the isolated worker model: 
Upgrade your app directly to .NET 10 by following:

  • Update Language Versions in Azure Functions 

Note: If your app is on a Linux Consumption plan, you will need to first upgrade to Flex Consumption plan before upgrading to .NET 10. 

Complete all required upgrades and ensure your app has moved off the in-process model before November 10, 2026. 

Learn more.

Title: Public Preview: Flex Nodes for AKS

Body.Content:
Flex Nodes for AKS is a deployment option for application and platform teams to use hybrid and edge infrastructure as connected worker nodes to an AKS control plane in Azure. Flex Nodes provide a consistent Kubernetes control plane while enabling teams to govern and secure compute for latency, regulatory, or sovereign needs. Rather than deploying an operating a complete Kubernetes cluster with a local control plane, Flex Nodes for AKS are designed for connected environments where only the worker nodes run at the edge or on customer infrastructure. Flex Nodes for AKS is ideal for applications that require local execution but not local operations, including AI inference, data processing, industrial applications, content delivery, branch office services, and latency-sensitive business workloads.

Learn more.

Title: Public Preview: Introducing a Guided Copilot Experience for Building Azure Apps in VS Code

Body.Content:
Today we're previewing a new way to build cloud apps with GitHub Copilot in VS Code: a guided Copilot experience that takes you from idea to a deployed Azure app through a structured, predictable workflow instead of a free-form chat session that may or may not land where you need it to.

The problem: Copilot is powerful, but unpredictable

Ask Copilot to "build me a Node.js API on Azure Functions with a Postgres database" today, and you might get a working project, or you might not. Sometimes Copilot scaffolds the app but skips infrastructure. Sometimes it generates a deployment script that fails halfway through. Sometimes it forgets what you were building three prompts later.

The underlying model is capable. The problem is the shape of the experience: an open-ended chat with no checkpoints, no guardrails, and no consistent path from "I have an idea" to "it's running in Azure."

Learn more: 

  • Read the blog 
  • Install the Azure Tools extension for VS Code

Title: Public Preview: Foundry Routines in Foundry Agent Service

Body.Content:
In public preview, Foundry Agent Service adds Foundry Routines, a native trigger primitive for running published agents automatically. Production agents often need to run on a schedule or when a business event occurs, and today that means assembling external glue such as Logic Apps, Azure Functions, webhooks, queues, custom storage, and separate identity and role assignments. 

The agent is governed in Foundry, but the trigger layer has been customer-owned infrastructure with its own configuration, monitoring, and failure modes. Routines includes recurring schedules, one-shot delayed timers, and event-based triggers through supported connections, keeping triggers, execution, and observability inside the governed Foundry workspace. The preview is intended for evaluation and is not covered by production SLAs. To get started, add a Routine to a published agent in Foundry Agent Service. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Enable and disable controls for Microsoft Foundry agents in Agent 365

Body.Content:

Administrators can control whether a Foundry agent is available for use across their organization using the same elevation pattern applied to comparable agent application actions, without requiring developer intervention. 

This fills a core governance gap by bringing Foundry agents into the Admin Center alongside other agent types, so IT and governance teams manage the full agent estate consistently and can meet compliance and security requirements around which agents are active. Broader Agent 365 and Microsoft Entra governance operations such as block, unblock, delete, restore, and owner reassignment continue to expand. To get started, open Microsoft Admin Center and use the Agent 365 governance controls. 

Learn more.

Body.Content:
In public preview, Microsoft Foundry now lets customers govern the outbound connections a hosted agent can make. Customers author ordered rules matched on destination host, including FQDN with wildcards such as *.contoso.com, with actions to allow, deny, transform outbound request headers, or rewrite the destination. Rules live in the agent's Responsible AI policy and are enforced inside the Foundry-managed agent sandbox before traffic leaves the runtime, so no separate network appliance is required for basic allow-listing. 

Two enforcement modes are supported: audit, which logs would-deny decisions without blocking, and enforce, which blocks denied traffic, letting teams observe real traffic before switching on enforcement. Every egress decision is emitted to Application Insights for audit. The preview is intended for evaluation and is not covered by production SLAs. To get started, configure egress controls under Guardrails in the Foundry portal. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Publishing Microsoft Foundry agents to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams

Body.Content:
Publishing Microsoft Foundry agents to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams is now generally available. An agent only delivers value once it reaches the people who need it, and Foundry developers previously had no native path to make their agents operational across Microsoft 365, requiring separate deployment pipelines, bot registrations, and app manifests. 

With this release you publish an agent directly into Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams, where it becomes discoverable to end users in the surfaces where they already work. Published agents remain governed through the same Microsoft Entra and Agent 365 controls IT uses for the rest of the organization, giving admins centralized visibility over their agent fleet from day one, so distribution does not mean giving up governance. To get started, publish your Foundry agent to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams from the Foundry portal. 

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: Logical replication slot sync status metric for Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server

Body.Content:
You can now monitor the synchronization status of your logical replication slots in Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible Server using the new logical_replication_slot_sync_status metric. This Azure Monitor metric shows whether each logical replication slot is synchronized, catching up, or in an unknown state, helping you validate replication health and slot readiness. 

This feature is especially useful when using logical decoding or change data capture (CDC) tools like Debezium or Kafka. With per-slot visibility and the ability to set up alerts, you can ensure your logical replication setup remains consistent and responsive during planned maintenance, migrations, or system events.

Title: Public Preview: Azure Payments HSM v2

Body.Content:
Azure Payments HSM v2 is a highly available, single-tenant Payment HSM service for payment processing, credential issuance, PIN processing, key management, and authentication data protection. Customers retain exclusive administrative control of an isolated, single-tenant Payment HSM cluster while Microsoft manages the underlying infrastructure, availability, and lifecycle operations. Azure Payments HSM v2 enables customers to protect sensitive payment assets, maintain key sovereignty, and meet the stringent security, compliance, audit, performance, and operational requirements of the Payment Card Industry (PCI). 

Azure Payment HSM v2 runs in PCI DSS and PCI 3DS compliant Azure data centers, on security infrastructure certified to FIPS 140-3 Level 3, PCI DSS, PCI 3DS, and PCI PIN (PTS). Because payment HSM clusters are isolated per customer, customers can deploy the service as a validated component within their own PCI solution, simplifying ongoing audit and compliance. 

Learn more.

Title: Public Preview: Azure Red Hat OpenShift with hosted control planes

Body.Content:
Azure Red Hat OpenShift with hosted control planes is now in public preview. It is a new deployment option for Azure Red Hat OpenShift that runs the OpenShift control plane as a fully managed service, separate from the worker nodes that run customer applications. 

Azure Red Hat OpenShift with hosted control planes accelerates application modernization by providing a fully managed OpenShift platform operated by Microsoft and Red Hat SREs, allowing teams to focus on building applications instead of managing infrastructure. Organizations can modernize at their own pace and run virtual machines, containers, and cloud-native applications on a single AI-ready platform.

This deployment model enables developers to move faster. Clusters provision in minutes, and development and test environments can scale down during idle periods and scale back up when needed. This helps teams to accelerate experimentation, shorten testing cycles, and bring applications to production more quickly while optimizing infrastructure spend. 

Azure Red Hat OpenShift with hosted control planes simplifies operations across growing multi-cluster environments by separating control plane and worker node lifecycles, giving organizations greater flexibility over application upgrades. Teams can scale across regions and environments, customize networking, and maintain operational consistency while Microsoft and Red Hat manage the underlying platform. 

Azure Red Hat OpenShift with hosted control planes strengthens security through managed identity and workload identity, using short-lived, automatically rotated tokens instead of stored credentials. Organizations can integrate with their existing identity providers and enhance compliance with default etcd encryption and bring-your-own- keys to meet data residency, sovereignty, and regulatory requirements. 

Public preview is available in UK South, Canada Central, Australia East, Switzerland North, Brazil South, Central India, East US 2, and West Europe. 

To get started, create a new Azure Red Hat OpenShift cluster with hosted control planes through the Azure CLI, REST API, or Bicep. Azure Red Hat OpenShift with standard architecture remains fully supported and actively developed.  

Learn more.

Title: Public Preview: PostgreSQL skills and MCP plugin for Azure Database for PostgreSQL

Body.Content:
The PostgreSQL skills and MCP plugin turns supported AI coding assistants into context-aware PostgreSQL experts that can both provide guidance and act on a connected database. The bundled plugin combines expert-curated skills for PostgreSQL and Azure Database for PostgreSQL with an MCP server that can inspect your live database context, run queries, apply changes, and support database operations.

It automatically routes between generic PostgreSQL and Azure-specific guidance based on your question and connection context.

The plugin is available through supported AI coding assistants, including GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code, and Codex CLI.

Title: Announcing: New Windows App client-side endpoints for Azure Virtual Desktop

Body.Content:
Beginning in early October 2026, Windows App will begin using three new wildcard fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) for client-side service traffic to Azure Virtual Desktop. These domains are already included in the cloud-side connectivity requirements. If your organization applies network controls to devices running Windows App, you must allow these endpoints before activation. If the endpoints are not reachable, users may experience sign-in and connection failures.  

This is a client-side change for Windows App and is separate from the previous cloud-side domain update. Organizations that have already completed the cloud-side update should still review proxy, firewall, VPN, DNS filtering, and Secure Web Gateway policies that apply to user devices to ensure these endpoints are allowed.

This work is part of a wider Microsoft approach to unify domain requirements.

Required client-side endpoints

*.windows.cloud.microsoft 

  • Purpose: General Windows cloud service traffic

  • Port: 443/TCP

*.service.windows.cloud.microsoft 

  • Purpose: Service traffic which requires optimization

  • Port: 443/TCP

*.windows.static.microsoft 

  • Purpose: Static content, installation, and update assets

  • Port: 443/TCP

Timeline

Windows App will begin using these endpoints in early October 2026. 

Who is affected?

Organizations that:

  • Use Windows App to connect to Azure Virtual Desktop.

  • Apply firewall, proxy, VPN, DNS filtering, Secure Web Gateway, or similar controls to end-user devices.

Potential Impact 

If these endpoints are unavailable, blocked, or inspected in a way that interrupts the connection, users may experience failures during sign-in, resource discovery, connection, or an active session.

Recommended Action

Before early October 2026:

  • Allow outbound HTTPS traffic on 443/TCP to all three FQDNs in applicable firewall rules, proxy allow lists, VPN configurations, DNS filters, and Secure Web Gateway policies.

  • Review TLS inspection or other traffic interception that could prevent Windows App from reaching Microsoft services. Where permitted by organizational policy, route this traffic directly to Microsoft.

  • If client devices are behind managed network boundary engage the team that manages those controls as early as possible, as approval and change-management processes may require additional lead time.

  • Inform your help desk and update internal network and troubleshoot guide.

Learn more:

  • Required FQDNs and endpoints for Azure Virtual Desktop

  • Microsoft unified cloud.microsoft domain

Title: Public Preview: HTTP/3 over QUIC support in Azure Application Gateway

Body.Content:
Announcing public preview support for HTTP/3 over QUIC on Azure Application Gateway. HTTP/3 is the next evolution of HTTP and uses QUIC to improve connection setup time, reduce latency, and provide better resiliency for modern web applications and APIs. 

With HTTP/3 support, Application Gateway can now serve frontend client connections over QUIC, helping improve performance for latency-sensitive workloads such as web applications, messaging platforms, mobile experiences, transactions, and APIs. QUIC reduces connection establishment overhead and supports independent streams, helping minimize the impact of packet loss and improving responsiveness over unreliable or high-latency networks. 

HTTP/3 is configured at the listener level, allowing you to enable it selectively on Basic listeners. During public preview, HTTP/3 can be configured by using the Azure portal or through the REST API. 

Learn more.

Title: Retirement: Azure Linux with OS Guard in Azure Kubernetes Service

Body.Content:
Support for Azure Linux with OS Guard in Azure Kubernetes Service will end on December 10, 2026. Azure Container Linux is the replacement for Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview). Starting on December 10, 2026:
  • Users won’t be able to create new Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview) node pools.
  • AKS won’t produce new node images for affected node pools.
  • Existing node pools won’t receive security patches.
On March 10, 2027, AKS will remove the Azure Linux with OS Guard node images. After the images are removed, scaling and remediation operations, including reimage and redeploy operations, will fail for affected node pools. You can use either of the following migration options:
  • Migrate an existing Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool in place by following the Migrate nodes to Azure Container Linux for Azure Kubernetes Service documentation. This operation preforms a standard node image upgrade.
  • Alternatively, create a new Azure Container Linux node pool, migrate and validate workloads, and then delete the Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool. Follow Add Azure Container Linux node pools and remove existing node pools.
For other available options, see the AKS node operating system. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A or AKS GitHub Repository. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

Title: Public Preview: Agentless migration of on-premises SMB file shares to Azure Files (SMB)

Body.Content:
Azure Storage Mover now supports agentless migration of on-premises SMB file shares to Azure Files (SMB), in public preview. You can move file data from Windows Server or NAS shares into Azure without deploying, registering, or maintaining a migration agent on-premises.

With agentless migration, the Storage Mover service connects directly to your SMB share over your existing private connection (VPN or ExpressRoute) and copies data to the destination Azure file share. Source credentials are stored securely in Azure Key Vault, and Storage Mover's managed identities handle access to both the source secrets and the target share. Configure source and target endpoints, create a job, and start the copy from the Azure portal or Azure CLI.

Agentless SMB migration joins Storage Mover's existing agent-based paths for SMB and NFS sources, giving you more flexibility to modernize file storage on your own terms.

Learn more.

Title: Generally Available: User-bound user delegation SAS for Azure Storage

Body.Content:
Announcing the addition of enhanced secure authentication in Azure Storage that combines the flexibility of user-delegation shared access signature (SAS) with the user-bound access of Entra ID. User-bound user delegation SAS is now generally available for all regions. 

User delegation SAS is an existing feature that allows users to create secure SAS tokens that are tied to the delegator, meaning the delegator must verify their identity with Entra to create the token. The resulting token can be traced to the delegator and can only be valid for up to 7 days. This feature is an extension of user delegation (UD) SAS, which is already generally available for Azure Blobs, Azure Files, Azure Tables, and Azure Queues. User-bound user delegation SAS allows users to create a more secure SAS token than account SAS, service SAS, or normal user delegation SAS by restricting the usage of the SAS token to an end user identity. This will help enforce that the user delegated SAS can only be used by intended users.  

There is no additional cost to use user-bound user delegation SAS. Pricing is based on standard transaction costs for your storage account type, refer to Azure Storage Pricing for details. 

This feature is available in all public regions.

Learn more:

  •  Create a user delegation SAS 
  •  Read the announcement blog

User-bound user delegation SAS allows users to create a more secure SAS token than account SAS, service SAS, or normal user delegation SAS by restricting the usage of the SAS token to an end user identity. This will help enforce that the user delegated SAS can only be used by intended users .

There is no additional cost to use user-bound user delegation SAS. Pricing is based on standard transaction costs for your storage account type, refer to Azure Storage Pricing for details.

This feature is available in all public regions.

Title: Generally Available: Azure Ephemeral OS Disk with full caching for VM/VMSS

Body.Content:
Azure Ephemeral OS Disk with full caching is now generally available for new virtual machines and Virtual Machine Scale Sets. The capability caches the complete OS image on a VM’s local storage, eliminating remote-storage reads after caching finishes. This delivers consistently fast, low-millisecond OS disk access, up to 10× better I/O performance, and greater resilience during storage interruptions—without slowing VM provisioning because caching runs asynchronously after boot. It is designed for I/O-sensitive, stateless workloads such as AI training and inference, quorum-based databases, real-time analytics, and large-scale services. Full caching uses a VM’s cache, resource, or NVMe disk and reduces available local capacity by twice the OS disk size.


It is available across Azure public regions for supported 8-core-and-larger GPU, storage-optimized, memory-optimized, HPC, general-purpose, and compute-optimized VM series. Customers can enable it through Azure CLI, ARM templates, or REST APIs by setting the full-caching option for Ephemeral OS disks.

Title: Public Preview: Azure Front Door profile and route level WAF policies

Body.Content:
Azure Front Door’s Web Application Firewall (WAF) now supports profile and route level WAF policy associations in public preview. This gives you more flexibility to apply broad baseline protection across an Azure Front Door profile while using targeted policies for specific applications, domains, or routes that need different controls. 

With this update, you can associate WAF policies at the profile, domain, or route scope. For example, you can use a profile level policy for common protections across all domains in a profile, then apply a route level policy to sensitive paths such as sign-in, checkout, or API routes. This helps reduce policy duplication while still allowing more granular security configuration where it's needed. 

If multiple WAF policy scopes apply to a request, Azure Front Door uses the most specific policy: a route level policy takes precedence over a domain level policy, and a domain level policy takes precedence over a profile level policy. To get started, create or update an Azure Front Door WAF policy in the Azure portal and choose the associated scope that matches your deployment needs. 

Learn more.
